title: The yoga of despair
hookLine: the last argument, the last verse of chapter one, and a warrior sitting down in the middle of the field
carry: despair, too, is counted as a yoga

cards: Some people know this moment. Weeks of holding it together, every argument made, to themselves and to everyone else. Then, one ordinary afternoon, in a parking lot or a kitchen or an office bathroom, they just sit down.
Not because they decided to. Because they can't stand up anymore. That's where chapter one of the Gita ends.
Not with a battle, but with the warrior Krishna drove into the middle of the field sitting down in his chariot, his bow on the floor.

teach.b: Arjuna's last arguments, in verses forty to forty-four, are about what a war like this destroys beyond the dead.
When a family is wiped out, he says, its old ways die with it: the rites, the offerings to the ancestors, the order that held a society together. Chaos follows, and the generations after are lost.

It's the argument of a man from his own time and world, and people read it differently today: some commentators hear real grief for everything a war erases, some hear a mind grabbing any argument it can find.
Either way, it ends in a cry. Alas, he says, we're about to commit a great wrong, killing our own people out of greed for a kingdom.

teach.h: BETTER IF THEY KILLED ME UNARMED.
teach.b: Then the line that's hardest to hear: it would be better for me if the sons of Dhritarashtra, weapons in hand, killed me in battle, unarmed and not fighting back.
And Sanjaya, telling the blind king, describes what he sees. In Sanskrit: visrijya sasharam chapam shoka samvigna manasah.
Casting aside his bow and arrows, his mind shaken with grief, Arjuna sinks down onto the seat of his chariot, there between the two armies. That's the end of chapter one. And here's the surprise.
Every chapter of the Gita has a title calling it a yoga, a path.
This one is Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the yoga of Arjuna's despair. Despair, counted as a path. None of Krishna's teaching happens without this.

teach.h: THE BOOK BEGINS WITH I CAN'T.
teach.b: The book begins because a man sat down and said, I can't.

how: Chapter one of the Gita is traditionally titled Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the yoga of Arjuna's despair; many readers and teachers treat Arjuna's collapse at 1.47 as the necessary starting point for the teaching that follows.

practice: Think of something you've been carrying and fighting with for too long, and picture it as a bow, heavy in your hands.
Without deciding anything about tomorrow, set it down, let your hands be empty, and sit, the way Arjuna sits in his chariot. You don't have to fix anything yet.
And if I can't ever turns into thoughts of hurting yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number, today.
